clause-position.rule_summary: A statement clause is the user's when its "I" is the first or second word of the clause. Clauses are split only at , ; : and the existing sentence ends; one word may come before "I" ("Lately I", "So I"), but no more, because putting words in the user's mouth takes a speaker and a verb ("my friend says I"). The "I" must be inside the quote itself. Where the quote was cut from mid-sentence, the words the user said in front of it count toward the position, so context can only take a clause away, never add one. A clause is also dropped when it opens inside a quotation mark, or when one of the gate's existing _HYPOTHETICAL_MARKERS starts before its "I" anywhere earlier in the sentence ("maybe I'll", "if I ever …, I'd"). Questions are kept whole as before, and the rule keeps clauses one by one, not whole sentences.

attack-first.rule_summary: A question still raises its topic, and a statement still needs the pronoun "I" in the quote, as in D-33. Each statement is now judged on the whole sentence it was cut from in the user's turn, so a quote cut down to "I should do a full marathon" is still read with its "My friend says". A sentence is dropped if it carries the gate's own _HYPOTHETICAL_MARKERS, or if it has "if I" plus another "I" followed by an auxiliary such as would, 'll or have to (D-46). Inside a sentence (split into clauses at , ; : dashes and before and/but/so/or), a clause is someone else's and is removed in three cases: its "I" comes right after "me"; or something other than "I" opens the clause and its first "I" takes should/would/'d/could/may/might/ought; or a person word (he/she/they/you/everyone/someone, or a possessive like my/our) opens the clause and its first "I" takes will/'ll/must/need or "have to"/"going to" (D-41). The sentence raises its topic only if a clause of the user's own keeps its "I" inside the quote. Clauses with no "I" stay as context, as before. The rule only removes text: it never returns a word D-33 would not.
